lines: Scattered sheep make the whole day longer than it needs to be.
Wolves near the pens change how everyone <pulse>listens after dark</pulse>.
Clean wool is quiet proof that somebody did the dull work well.
Warmth is easy to praise after someone else made it.
A good blanket is village peace you can fold.
Patterns are easier to see when you stop yanking the thread.
Most days, I am at the loom, trying to keep flocks and weather from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think wool is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good shears more than a loud promise. The shears has less to prove.
A flock teaches patience by spreading out exactly when you relax.
Wool looks soft, but the work behind it has elbows.
Sheep remember holes in fences better than people do.
A calm flock is usually a sign that someone worried early.
Good wool starts with dry shelter and fewer surprises.
You learn the weather by watching ears, hooves, and the sky in that order.
The loom makes patience visible, one thread at a time.
A village sleeps warmer because somebody counted carefully.
Shepherding is mostly noticing who is missing before missing becomes danger.
A fence is a promise with posts in it.
Wool gathers every scent and half the day's mistakes.
If the flock is quiet, I check twice. Silence can be planning.
The best blanket is remembered only when the night turns cold.
I trust steady wool more than fancy talk.
A sheep can find trouble in an empty field. It is a gift, apparently.
That boat ride was calm enough, until I remembered I was trusting you with the shore.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.
When I followed you through {follow_biome}, I finally understood why sheep wander off quietly.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to ask more questions before walking.
A flock knows danger before pride admits it. I listen to the woolly experts.
Dye work teaches patience. So does convincing sheep that the gate is not a puzzle.
Warm beds start as quiet animals and careful hands.
Most days, I am at the loom, trying to keep flocks and weather from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think wool is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
I trust a good shears more than a loud promise. The shears has less to prove.
If one sheep goes quiet, I notice. Quiet sheep are usually planning something.
